title: Localizations of smooth fine-monoid maps and affine smooth product charts
statement:
Use fine integral commutative monoids, their spectra, localization and local homomorphisms as in [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup], and fine monoschemes and their smooth morphisms as in [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. If a local homomorphism $\phi:P\to Q$ extends to an isomorphism $P\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s\simeq Q$ over $P$, and $P',Q'$ are localizations for which $\phi$ extends to a local homomorphism $P'\to Q'$, then this extended homomorphism is again of that form for some finite nonnegative ranks.

Every point $x$ of a fine monoscheme $X$ has a smallest open neighborhood $X_x$ consisting of its generalizations, canonically isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}_{\rm mon}\mathcal M_{X,x}$ with its ordinary monoid sheaf. For any smooth morphism $f:Y\to X$ and $y\in Y$, put $x=f(y)$ and $P=\mathcal M_{X,x}$. There are finite $r,s\geq0$ and an isomorphism $Y_y\simeq\operatorname{Spec}_{\rm mon}(P\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s)$ under which $Y_y\to X_x$ is induced by the first-factor inclusion. Conversely, a morphism covered by such affine product charts is smooth.

For fine fans the same assertions hold with sharp stalks and sharpened structure sheaves: a smooth stalk map $P\to P\oplus\mathbf N^r$ stays of this form after localization and sharpening, and every smooth fan morphism is covered by the corresponding affine product charts. No torsion-freeness hypothesis is required.

source.place: Expose VIII 3.1.4(iii), 3.1.9--3.1.10(ii), 3.1.13--3.1.16, printed pp.98--100; Lemma 3.1.14 and Remark 3.1.16. No Stacks tag states this monoidal-space result.

proof.text: First justify the single-denominator reductions, including for arbitrary localizations. If $L=A-S$ is a localization of a fine monoid $A$, put $E=A\cap L^\times$. A sum is a unit in any commutative monoid exactly when both summands are units, so $E$ is a face. For a fixed finite generating list of $A$, an expression for an element of $E$ uses only generators in $E$. Let $a$ be their sum, allowing $a=0$. Each such generator has inverse $(a-e_i)-a$ in $A_a$. Thus every element of $E$ is inverted in $A_a$, while $a$ is already a unit in $L$ and $S\subseteq E$. The inclusions inside $A^{\mathrm{gp}}$ give $L=A-E=A_a$. This localization is fine: it is generated by the generators of $A$ together with $-a$, and is integral as a submonoid of $A^{\mathrm{gp}}$.

source.place: VIII 3.1.2, p.98; the single-denominator assertion used in Lemma 3.1.14

proof.text:
Identify $Q=P\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s$ over $P$. Write $P'=P_a$ by step 1. Since $a$ is invertible in $Q'$, first invert $(a,0,0)$ in $Q$ to obtain $Q_a=P_a\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s$. The monoid $Q'$ is a further localization of $Q_a$; write it as $(Q_a)_b$ by step 1, with $b=(p,n,z)$. Because $b$ is a unit in $Q'$, its summand $(p,0,0)$ is a unit there. Localness of $P_a\to Q'$ implies $p\in P_a^\times$. Hence inverting $b$ only inverts $n$ in the free factor. If $J=\{i:n_i>0\}$ and $t=|J|$, then
$$ (\mathbf N^r)_n=\{v\in\mathbf Z^r:v_i\geq0\ (i\notin J)\}=\mathbf N^{r-t}\oplus\mathbf Z^t.$$
Indeed every $v$ in the middle set has $v+kn\in\mathbf N^r$ for sufficiently large $k$, and every fraction $m-kn$ has nonnegative coordinates outside $J$. Consequently $Q'\simeq P'\oplus\mathbf N^{r-t}\oplus\mathbf Z^{s+t}$ over $P'$. This proves the localization assertion, including $n=0$ and zero ranks.

source.place: VIII Lemma 3.1.14, p.100; explicit free-factor calculation

proof.text: For an affine chart $A(A)\subset X$ containing $x$, let $\mathfrak p$ represent $x$. The prime-minimal-neighborhood lemma gives $X_x=D(b)$, where $b$ is the sum of chart generators outside $\mathfrak p$, and $A_b=A_{\mathfrak p}$. It is smallest in all of $X$: intersect any neighborhood with this chart first. By definition of generalization, membership in every neighborhood of $x$ is exactly being a generalization of $x$. The structure-sheaf prescription gives $\Gamma(D(b),\mathcal M)=A_b$, and the germ map to $\mathcal M_{X,x}$ is an isomorphism since $D(b)$ is the smallest neighborhood. To identify the whole monoidal space, the homomorphism $A\to A_b$ gives $A(A_b)\to A(A)$ by the unsharpened spectrum universal property; its image lies in $D(b)$ since $b$ is a unit. Conversely $A_b=\Gamma(D(b),\mathcal M)$ gives $D(b)\to A(A_b)$. Their composites are identities by the same universal property and their maps on canonical sections (for the composite on $D(b)$ compose with its open inclusion into $A(A)$). Thus $X_x\simeq A(\mathcal M_{X,x})$ canonically, with the ordinary structure sheaf. All localization identifications act identically on germs, so this description is independent of the initial chart.

Let $f:Y\to X$, $y\in Y$ and $x=f(y)$. Continuity sends generalizations of $y$ to generalizations of $x$, so $f$ restricts to $Y_y\to X_x$. Under step 3 the section maps are exactly the stalk map, because each germ map from the smallest neighborhood is an isomorphism and restriction commutes with germs. If $f$ is smooth, its defining stalk condition supplies an isomorphism $P\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s\simeq\mathcal M_{Y,y}$ over $P=\mathcal M_{X,x}$. The unsharpened spectrum universal property now identifies the restricted morphism with the first-factor chart in the statement, including its sheaf homomorphism. Conversely, for any chart induced by $P\to Q=P\oplus\mathbf N^r\oplus\mathbf Z^s$, the stalk map at a point is $P_{\mathfrak p}\to Q_{\mathfrak q}$ with $\mathfrak p$ the inverse image of $\mathfrak q$ (the explicit stalk formula in that universal property). It is local, and step 2 makes it smooth. Every point lying in such a chart therefore satisfies the defining stalk condition. The neighborhoods $Y_y$ cover $Y$.

source.place: VIII 3.1.15 and Remark 3.1.16(i), p.100; Lemma 3.1.8(i), p.99

proof.text:
For sharp $P$ and a local product inclusion $P\to P\oplus\mathbf N^r$, apply step 2 before sharpening to localizations $P'\to Q'$. It gives $Q'\simeq P'\oplus\mathbf N^{r-t}\oplus\mathbf Z^t$ over $P'$. Units in this direct product are exactly $P'^\times\oplus\{0\}\oplus\mathbf Z^t$: a nonnegative coordinate can have an additive inverse only if it is zero. Taking quotients by these units therefore gives
$$\overline{Q'}\simeq\overline{P'}\oplus\mathbf N^{r-t}$$
over $\overline{P'}$. The same argument works with an initial lattice factor, which disappears on sharpening. This is the sharp localization assertion. Only the stated product decomposition is used; no splitting of an arbitrary fine monoid by its unit group is asserted.

For a fine fan use the existing point-localization theorem: $X_x$ and $Y_y$ are the smallest affine neighborhoods with their sharp stalk monoids and sharpened sheaves, and their germ homomorphisms are isomorphisms. A smooth stalk map is $P\to P\oplus\mathbf N^r$ by definition. The sharp affine-spectrum universal property, natural in source and target, identifies the restricted fan morphism with its first-factor chart, because its section homomorphism is this stalk map. Conversely consider such a sharp chart and any point of its source. On ordinary spectra its underlying map is prime contraction: the inverse image of a prime is determined by which canonical sections have nonzero germs. The sharp localization-section theorem identifies its stalk map with the sharpened localizations of $P\to P\oplus\mathbf N^r$; the ordinary localized map is local since the primes contract. Step 5 makes this sharp stalk map a product inclusion. Hence these fan charts are smooth, and a morphism covered by them is smooth. This also proves the claimed fan form with the sharpened structure sheaves. All ranks are finite, and none of these arguments impose torsion-freeness.

source.place: VIII Remark 3.1.10(ii), 3.1.15 and Remark 3.1.16(ii), pp.99--100; Lemma 3.1.8(ii), p.99

split_report.summary: Proved the localization claim by explicit finite-denominator and free-coordinate calculations; proved unsharpened affine stalk neighborhoods and smooth charts, and treated sharp fans separately using the existing sharp-spectrum nodes. Step 1 (3.1.2): a localization of a fine monoid equals a single-element localization A_a, using the face E = A ∩ L^× and the inverse (a-e_i)-a. Step 2 follows the proof of Lemma 3.1.14 exactly: p is a unit by locality, and (N^r)_n = N^{r-t} ⊕ Z^t, checked in both directions and with n = 0, t = r and zero ranks. Step 3: lem-trf-monoid-prime-minimal-neighborhood gives the smallest D(b) with A_b = A_p, and the universal property of the new node gives the isomorphism D(b) ≅ A(A_b); both composites check out. Step 4 (3.1.15-3.1.16(i)): in the forward direction both morphisms correspond to the same map P → Γ; in the converse the new node's stalk formula gives a local localization, and step 2 then gives smoothness. Step 5: the units of the product are P'^× ⊕ 0 ⊕ Z^t, so sharpening gives the sharp form; no unit-group splitting is used, so torsion is harmless. Step 6 uses the statements of lem-trf-fine-fan-point-localization, lem-trf-affine-fan-hom-universal (all its sharp hypotheses hold) and lem-trf-affine-fan-localization-sections; the point map is prime contraction, and step 5 makes each stalk map a product inclusion. The new node lem-trf-monoid-spectrum-hom-universal is ILO VIII Lemma 3.1.8(i). It is true: 𝔭_t is a prime ideal, the map is continuous, and the stalk map is local. I tested it with P = 0, Z/2 and Z and with T empty. It is not a duplicate: the existing nodes (affine-fan-hom-universal, canonical-section-rigidity, germ-rigidity, basic-map-local-lift) all need sharp targets and sharp stalks.
